# Earned beginnings and a reason to continue

The opening failed because it supplied the end state of a relationship before showing its beginning. Three followers, a catalogue of powers and a stock of supplies implied histories that the player had never lived. Removing numbers alone would not solve this; the player also needs a local identity, a reason to move, a reason for the first companion to risk something, and a question that survives the first rescue. The implementation now begins with Sable as a civilian courier, alone at home, with an ordinary delivery entrusted to him.

The comparative notebook is a targeted study of six games and eight retrieved sources, with explicit coverage in sources.json. It is not a claim to have ingested every popular RPG, nor an experiment proving that a narrative pattern causes retention. Chrono Trigger supplies the useful contrast between everyday social encounters and a larger crisis, as well as a complete route outline in which earlier events motivate later destinations and personal quests. FFVII Remake supplies an important counterexample to the idea that all games must begin powerless: a competent protagonist can be convincing when the mission, opposition and consequences are clear. Its civilian aftermath matters to our voice-extraction plot.

The FFVI interview is useful for character-specific context, emotional contrast and music as drama; it is not a complete FFVI plot analysis. Xenoblade 3’s developers explain an alliance through a common oppressive condition and different backgrounds, supporting our decision to make joining an act of commitment. The Hades interview and developer FAQ support evolving relationships, retained progress after failure and meaningful combinations; their lesson is to make players want the next scene and next experiment while still offering resolution. Toby Fox’s own Undertale design account emphasizes enemy combinations, freshness and moving on after mastery. That argues for a short, instructive first encounter rather than a repetitive experience wall. These applications are design judgments, not quotations or statistical conclusions.

The implemented first sequence is home, reed delivery, instrument repair, Nell’s father’s stolen voice, Rook’s deliberate alliance, recovered work tools, the first clay pattern, and Iona’s choice to help her patients. Sable begins with no money, no supplies, no learned personal techniques and no Mako slots. The parcel gives two home remedies; repairing the orchestra earns 20 credits. The workshop yields basic work gear rather than an unexplained armory. Reading the plate grants Earth/Focus and one socket. Iona’s recruitment introduces healing. Clearing the yard earns the next support and a reinforced coat. Later rewards have a source in the chapter’s fiction: Link waits until the third chapter, a third socket until the sixth, and the full vocabulary emerges over the early campaign. The actual schedule is REWARDS in opening.js.

A first mystery without a payoff would merely defer the same hollowness. The newly recovered recording therefore has a defined arc: the archive exposes copied registrations, Sable later recognizes his courier mark, and the cracked clay distinguishes recording sessions from a secretly surviving person. The final decision concerns what to do with a freely given song, not which machine should own another person. Both choices return the reed case to the same home where the journey began. Mara acknowledges the player’s decision. Sable’s uniform chapter also changes his appearance, giving an existing narrative beat a visible consequence.

The existing 24 chapters remain the campaign. campaign-integration.json indexes their real debriefs, recruited characters and our new payoffs across three acts. Those debriefs were previously stored but largely skipped by the enhanced runtime; they are now shown and recorded. The journal retains discoveries, recruitment reasons, chapter consequences and retry context. Legacy saves keep their earned resources and existing party; the new beginning applies to New Game. No native SNES authoring or classic-edition saves are rewritten by this browser-engine pass.

Our next evidence must come from play, not from another spreadsheet pretending to measure fun. The hypotheses in campaign-integration.json ask whether players can state their goal, explain each recruitment, use the first tools, pursue the recording question and voluntarily return after a resolution. Initial timing, abandonment points, confusion and chosen return visits need observation with real players. Automated gates and encounter simulations establish consistency and reachability; they do not establish that the game is compelling or optimal.
